source_text: Προφανεῖς μὲν οὖν καὶ πᾶσαι αἱ ἄλλαι ἀρεταί, αἱ παρὰ τῷ Μωυσεῖ ἀναγεγραμμέναι, ἀρχὴν Ἕλλησι παντὸς τοῦ ἠθικοῦ τόπου παρασχόμεναι, ἀνδρείαν λέγω καὶ σωφροσύνην καὶ φρόνησιν καὶ δικαιοσύνην καρτερίαν τε καὶ ὑπομονὴν καὶ τὴν σεμνότητα καὶ ἐγκράτειαν τήν τε ἐπὶ τούτοις εὐσέβειαν. ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν εὐσέβεια παντί που δήλη τὸ ἀνωτάτω καὶ πρεσβύτατον αἴτιον σέβειν καὶ τιμᾶν καὶ διδάσκουσα. καὶ δικαιοσύνην δὲ αὐτὸς ὁ νόμος παρίστησι παιδεύων τήν τε φρόνησιν διὰ τῆς τῶν αἰσθητῶν εἰδώλων ἀποχῆς καὶ τῆς πρὸς τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τῶν ὅλων προσκληρώσεως, ἀφ’ ἧς δόξης οἷον πηγῆς πᾶσα σύνεσις αὔξεται. θυσίαι γὰρ ἀνόμων βδέλυγμα κυρίῳ, εὐχαὶ δὲ κατευθυνόντων δεκταὶ παρ’ αὐτῷ. ἐπεὶ οιαῦτα καὶ τὰ παρὰ Ἡσαΐᾳ· τί μοι πλῆθος τῶν θυσιῶν ὑμῶν ὑμῶν; λέγει κύριος, καὶ πᾶσα ἡ περικοπή· λῦε πάντα σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας· αὕτη γὰρ θυσία θεῷ δεκτή, καρδία συντετριμμένη καὶ ζητοῦσα τὸν πεπλακότα. ζυγὰ δόλια βδέλυγμα ἔναντι θεοῦ, στάθμιον δὲ δίκαιον δεκτὸν αὐτῷ. ἐντεῦθεν ζυγὸν μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν Πυθαγόρας παραινεῖ. δικαιοσύνη δὲ δολία εἴρηται ἡ τῶν αἱρέσεων ἐπαγγελία, καὶ γλῶσσα μὲν ἀδίκων ἐξολεῖται, στόμα δὲ δικαίων ἀποστάζει σοφίαν. ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοὺς σοφοὺς καὶ φρονίμους φαύλους καλοῦσιν. μακρὸν δ’ ἂν εἴη περὶ τῶν ἀρετῶν τούτων μαρτυρίας παρατίθεσθαι, ἁπάσης ταύτας ἐξυμνούσης τῆς γραφῆς. ἐπεὶ δ’ οὖν τὴν μὲν ἀνδρείαν ὁρίζονται ἐπιστήμην δεινῶν καὶ οὐ δεινῶν καὶ τῶν μεταξύ, τὴν δὲ σωφροσύνην ἕξιν ἐν αἱρέσει καὶ φυγῇ σῴζουσαν τὰ τῆς φρονήσεως κρίματα, παράκειται τε τῇ μὲν ἀνδρείᾳ ἥ τε ὑπομονή, ἣν καρτερίαν καλοῦσιν, ἐπιστήμην ἐμμενετέων καὶ οὐκ ἐμμενετέων, ἥ τε μεγαλοψυχία, ἐπιστήμη τῶν συμβαινόντων ὑπεραίρουσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῇ σωφροσύνῃ ἡ εὐλάβεια, ἔκκλισις οὖσα σὺν λόγῳ. Φυλακὴ δὲ τῶν ἐντολῶν, τήρησις οὖσα αὐτῶν ἀβλαβής, περιποίησίς ἐστιν ἀσφαλείας βίου. καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄνευ ἀνδρείας καρτερικὸν εἶναι οὐδὲ μὴν ἄνευ σωφροσύνης ἐγκρατῆ. ἀντακολουθοῦσι δὲ ἀλλήλαις αἱ ἀρεταί, καἰ παρ’ ᾧ αἱ τῶν ἀρετῶν ἀκολουθίαι, παρὰ τούτῳ καὶ ἡ σωτηρία, τήρησις οὖσα τοῦ εὖ ἔχοντος. εἰκότως ἔτι περὶ τούτων διαλαβόντες τῶν ἀρετῶν περὶ πασῶν ἂν εἴημεν ἐσκεμμένοι, ὅτι ὁ μίαν ἔχων ἀρετὴν γνωστικῶς πάσας ἔχει διὰ τὴν ἀντακολουθίαν. αὐτίκα ἡ ἐγκράτεια διάθεσίς ἐστιν ἀνυπέρβατος τῶν κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον φανέντων. ἐγκρατεύεται δὲ ὁ κατέχων τὰς παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον ὁρμὰς ἢ ὁ κατέχων αὑτὸν ὥστε μὴ ὁρμᾶν παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον.
thought_title: Virtues in Greek and Christian Thought
pass_a_gloss: The other virtues, which are written by Moses, are evident and they provide a starting point for all ethical matters for the Greeks, I mean courage and self-control and prudence and justice and patience and perseverance and dignity and self-control and the piety that is based on these. But piety is evident to everyone as the highest and most ancient cause to reverence and honor and to teach. And the law itself presents justice, teaching prudence through the avoidance of sensory idols and the calling to the creator and father of all, from which glory, as from a source, all understanding increases. For sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of those who are guided are acceptable to him. Since also the things from Isaiah say: what is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord, and the whole passage says: loose every bond of injustice, for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a heart that is broken and seeking the one who has been afflicted. False balances are an abomination before God, but a just scale is acceptable to him. From this, Pythagoras advises not to exceed the balance. But justice is said to be false, the promise of the sects, and the tongue of the unjust is destroyed, but the mouth of the just drips with wisdom. But they call the wise and prudent ones worthless. It would be long to present testimonies about these virtues, which all of scripture praises. Since, then, they define courage as the knowledge of what is fearful and not fearful and what is in between, and self-control as a state that saves the judgments of prudence in choice and avoidance, perseverance, which they call patience, is placed beside courage, as the knowledge of what is to be endured and not to be endured, and magnanimity, as the knowledge that surpasses what happens, but also caution is placed beside self-control, as a withdrawal with reason. The guarding of the commandments, being the blameless keeping of them, is the acquisition of the safety of life. And it is not possible to be patient without courage or self-controlled without self-control. The virtues follow one another, and where there are the followings of the virtues, there is also salvation, being the keeping of what is well-ordered. It is reasonable that, having taken up these virtues, we would be concerned with all of them, because the one who has one virtue knowingly has all of them through their mutual following. Immediately, self-control is a disposition that is invincible regarding the things that appear according to the right reason. And one is self-controlled who holds back the impulses that are contrary to the right reason or who holds back oneself so as not to be impelled contrary to the right reason.

choices.why: The verb ἐγκρατεύεται is in the present tense, indicating a state of being.
The phrase ὀρθὸν λόγον refers to the correct or proper reason.
The noun ἀντακολουθίαν refers to the mutual or reciprocal following of the virtues.

bible_refs.note: The passage from Isaiah says: what is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord, and the whole passage says: loose every bond of injustice, for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a heart that is broken and seeking the one who has been afflicted.

pass_b_english: The virtues that Moses wrote about are clear for all to see, and they laid the groundwork for the Greeks in all matters of ethics. These virtues include courage, self-control, prudence, justice, patience, perseverance, dignity, and self-control, as well as the piety that is rooted in these qualities. What's more, piety is universally recognized as the most ancient and highest cause of reverence, honor, and teaching. The law itself teaches justice and prudence by warning against idolatry and encouraging us to turn to the Creator and Father of all, from whom our understanding and wisdom flow like a river from its source. As the Lord says through Isaiah (Isaiah 1:11-17), our sacrifices and rituals are meaningless if we don't live justly - in fact, they're detestable to Him. Instead, we should loosen every bond of injustice and seek a broken and contrite heart, for this is the kind of sacrifice that God accepts. Similarly, false balances are an abomination to God, while a just scale is pleasing to Him, which is why Pythagoras advised people not to cheat or exceed the balance. On the other hand, the so-called justice of the sects is false, and the words of the wicked will be silenced, while the words of the just will be filled with wisdom. Unfortunately, the world often calls the wise and prudent worthless. If we were to gather all the testimonies from scripture about these virtues, it would be a lengthy task, since the whole of scripture praises them. The virtues are defined in specific ways: courage, for instance, is the knowledge of what is and isn't fearful, as well as what falls in between, while self-control is the state of being that preserves our prudent judgments, guiding us in what we choose and what we avoid. Perseverance, also known as patience, goes hand in hand with courage, as it's the knowledge of what we should and shouldn't endure, and magnanimity is the knowledge that rises above circumstances. Meanwhile, caution is closely tied to self-control, as it's the wise and reasoned withdrawal from harmful things. To guard the commandments and keep them blamelessly is to ensure the safety of our lives. Without courage, we can't be patient, and without self-control, we can't be self-controlled. The virtues are interconnected, and where we find the followings of the virtues, we also find salvation, which is the preservation of a well-ordered life. It's only reasonable that, having taken up these virtues, we should be concerned with all of them, since having one virtue means we have all of them, thanks to their mutual interconnectedness. Self-control, in particular, is a disposition that is invincible when it comes to the things that align with right reason. To be self-controlled means to hold back our impulses and desires when they contradict right reason, or to hold ourselves back from acting on them. This is the kind of self-control that allows us to live a life that is pleasing to God.
